summary:
Nicaragua does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or transgender identity. Article 204 of the Criminal Code, added by socially conservative legislators to a bill originally drafted to protect women from rape, made it an offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment to "induce, promote, propagandize, or practice sex among persons of the same sex in a scandalous manner". President Violeta Chamorro signed it in July 1992 and the Supreme Court rejected an unconstitutionality challenge in March 1994. The provision's vagueness also made it usable against LGBT-rights organising and sexual-health work. The language was dropped when a new Penal Code took effect on 1 March 2008, and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender, and sexual offences under Criminal Code articles 168, 170, 172 and 175 are gender-neutral.

Formal legality does not produce protection. The US State Department's 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices records a police and parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against people perceived as opponents of the government, which authorities neither investigated nor prosecuted, and lists violence and threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex people among the country's significant human rights violations. The report's assessment is that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Violence against LGBT people is widely tolerated socially and not enforced legally. Attacks are largely unreported because victims fear retaliation and expect poor legal outcomes. Trans women are the group most frequently targeted. Police are documented among the aggressors, tied with family members in the 2022 count, and assaults occur mainly in the street and in private homes.

The crackdown on protests that began in April 2018 left at least 325 people dead and more than 2,000 injured according to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. Amnesty International reported in May 2019 that journalist Miguel Mora was beaten by a pro-government mob and was targeted partly because he is gay, an instance of homophobia operating inside the political repression.

Marriage, partnership and adoption are restricted to heterosexual couples under the revised Family Code approved by Congress in June 2014 and in force from 8 April 2015; Article 72 of the Constitution defines marriage and stable unions as resting on the voluntary agreement of a man and a woman. A trans visitor travelling with a partner in a relationship read as same-sex under local law has no access to the legal benefits and protections available to married opposite-sex couples. Unconstitutionality actions were filed against the Family Code. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 holds that states party to the American Convention on Human Rights must give same-sex couples access to all domestic family-registration institutions, including marriage; no Nicaraguan implementation is recorded.

Ministerial Resolution 671-2014, adopted by the Ministry of Health and replacing Resolution 249-2009, requires non-discrimination in public and private health units on grounds of gender identity and gender expression, alongside sexual orientation. Article 3(l) of Law No. 820 prohibits discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds in the HIV and AIDS context.

Much of Nicaragua's media has been restricted since the 2018 protests and reporting is largely suppressed, which limits independent coverage of LGBT issues and makes the record of violence and enforcement harder to verify.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion is largely opposed to same-sex marriage. A Pew survey conducted between 9 November and 13 December 2013 found 77% opposed, 16% in favour and 7% unsure, and the 2017 AmericasBarometer recorded 24.5% support.

Visibility is uneven. Gay men are generally more visible in public than lesbians, who often socialise privately, and an annual Gay Pride celebration has been held in Managua around 28 June since the country's first public pride festival in 1991.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 sets a regional standard on family registration that Nicaraguan law does not meet, and no domestic implementing measure has followed.
localsOnly:
Article 315 of the Penal Code, which covers offences against labour rights, punishes discrimination based on "sexual option" with up to one year's imprisonment in employment.

Article 36(5) of the Penal Code makes discrimination based on sexual orientation an aggravating circumstance when any criminal offence is committed. The aggravator as described is framed on sexual orientation; no transgender-specific hate-crime aggravator is stated.

Couples whose relationship local law reads as same-sex, and households headed by such couples, are not eligible for the legal benefits and protections available to opposite-sex married couples. Congress approved the revised Family Code in June 2014 and it took effect on 8 April 2015, limiting marriage, partnerships and adoption to heterosexual couples; several organisations filed an action of unconstitutionality against it.
outOfScopeNotes:
F&M Global Barometers records no documented finding for Nicaragua.

No youth-specific findings on access to care are recorded.

No Nicaraguan implementation of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 is recorded.

The incidence of anti-LGBT violence is unresolved. Attacks are widely underreported out of fear of retaliation and because legal outcomes are poor, and no complete count is available.
